meter.explain: A time signature like 4/4 tells you how beats are grouped in a bar. Top number = beats per bar. Bottom number = which note value counts as one beat (4 = quarter note). 4/4 is the most common pop/rock/house feel: ONE-two-three-four. 3/4 is waltz: ONE-two-three. 6/8 feels like two bigger pulses, each split into three.

faq.q1: How do I find a song’s BPM with tap tempo?
faq.a1: Play the track and tap along with the beat in this tap BPM tool. After a few taps, BPM Tap averages your intervals into a live BPM counter reading. Keep tapping for a more stable value.
faq.a2: With steady tapping for 8–12 beats, most people land within about ±1–2 BPM of the true tempo — enough for DAW setup, DJ prep, and practice.
faq.a3: No. Everything runs in your browser. History stays on your device.
faq.a4: A BPM counter estimates beats per minute. This page is a tap tempo BPM counter: you tap the pulse, and the tool converts average tap gaps into BPM. Listen mode can also estimate tempo from your microphone without tapping.
faq.q5: Can I open delay or metronome at the same tempo?
faq.a5: Yes. Copy BPM, use Share link (?bpm=), or jump to Delay / Metronome from the related tools — the tempo can travel with the URL.
faq.q6: Can I find a song’s BPM with a microphone?
faq.a6: Yes. Open Listen, allow the mic, and play the track nearby. The tool estimates tempo in the browser — nothing is uploaded. Confirm with ÷2/×2, metronome, or refine by tapping.
delay.title: BPM Delay Calculator — Note Durations in ms
delay.description: Convert any BPM into delay and note lengths in milliseconds. Tap tempo built in; you can also paste a tempo from Listen mic BPM.
delay.h1: BPM delay calculator — note lengths in ms
delay.lead: Tap or set BPM, then copy note lengths in ms — straight, dotted, triplets.
delay.prose.title: Using delay ms in a DAW
delay.prose.1: Formula: ms per quarter note = 60,000 ÷ BPM. At 120 BPM a quarter is 500 ms; eighths are 250 ms; sixteenths are 125 ms.
delay.prose.2: Common picks: straight 1/8 for rhythmic echoes, dotted 1/8 for many slapbacks, 1/4 triplet for swung spaces. Copy a cell, paste into your delay plugin’s time field (ms mode).
delay.prose.3: Measure the song with tap tempo first, confirm with the metronome, then return here so the table matches the grid you actually want — including after ÷2 / ×2.
delay.faq.q1: How do I convert BPM to milliseconds?
delay.faq.a1: One beat in ms is 60,000 ÷ BPM. At 120 BPM a quarter note is 500 ms; half notes, 8ths, and 16ths scale from that. The table shows dotted and triplet lengths too.
delay.faq.q2: What delay time should I use for a slapback or 1/8 note?
delay.faq.a2: Use the 1/8 row for eighth-note echoes, or 1/8 dotted for many slapback feels. Tap the song first so the ms values match the track.
delay.faq.q3: Can I tap tempo on this page?
delay.faq.a3: Yes. Tap along with the beat, then copy any cell in the delay table. No signup — values stay in your browser.
metronome.title: Online Metronome — Accent, Time Signature & Tap Tempo
metronome.description: Free browser metronome with downbeat accent and time signatures (4/4, 3/4, 6/8…). Tap to set BPM — or bring a tempo from Listen mic detection — then click along.
metronome.lead: Tap to set BPM, pick a meter, hear a stronger click on beat one.
metronome.tips.1: Tap until Stable, then start the click — do not chase a moving number while practicing.
metronome.tips.2: Use accented beat one to feel bar lines in odd meters (5/4, 7/8) instead of counting aloud the whole time.
metronome.tips.3: If the click disagrees with the song, try ÷2 / ×2 — half-time and double-time feels are common.
metronome.faq.q1: How do I set the metronome BPM by tapping?
metronome.faq.a1: Tap the pad (or any key) in time with the song or the feel you want. When the reading stabilizes, start the metronome to confirm with an accented click.
metronome.faq.a2: Common practice meters: 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 5/4, 6/8, 7/8, 9/8, and 12/8. Beat one is accented louder/higher than the rest.
metronome.faq.q3: Is this metronome free to use in the browser?
metronome.faq.a3: Yes. No account and no install. Pair it with the tap BPM tool and delay calculator on BPM Tap when you need the full studio flow.

listen.prose.title: How mic BPM detection works
listen.prose.1: The tool listens for rhythmic energy (especially low-end hits), builds an onset curve, then scores likely tempos with autocorrelation — the same family of ideas used in classic beat trackers.
listen.prose.2: Room noise, quiet laptop speakers, and busy mixes can confuse any detector. Use headphones only if the track also plays into the room mic; otherwise point at a speaker. Try ÷2 / ×2 when the feel is half-time or double-time.
listen.prose.3: When the number looks right, start the metronome to confirm, copy BPM, or jump to Delay. Prefer tap tempo on the home tool if the room is too noisy.
listen.faq.q1: Can I find a song’s BPM with my microphone?
listen.faq.a1: Yes. Allow mic access, play the track nearby, and wait a few seconds for a live estimate. Then confirm with the metronome or refine by tapping.
listen.faq.a2: No. Analysis runs entirely in your browser. BPM Tap does not upload microphone audio.
listen.faq.q3: Why is the BPM sometimes double or half?
listen.faq.a3: Beat trackers often confuse the main pulse with half-time or double-time. Use ÷2 / ×2, pick an alternate candidate, or confirm against the metronome.
listen.faq.a4: Move closer to the speaker, reduce room noise, and give it 5–8 seconds. Electronic tracks with a clear kick usually work best.

pulse.h1: Online pulse counter — tap to get your heart rate
pulse.lead: No clock. No counting to sixty. Feel each heartbeat, tap once per beat, and read your BPM in seconds.
pulse.hint: Finger on pulse, other hand on the pad — or any key
pulse.howto.title: How to check your pulse with this tool
pulse.howto.1: Sit or stand still. Find your pulse on the wrist (radial) or neck (carotid) with two fingers — not the thumb.
pulse.howto.2: Tap the pad once for every heartbeat you feel. Keep the rhythm even.
pulse.howto.3: After several steady taps, copy or save the BPM. No second hand needed.
pulse.rules.title: Rules for measuring pulse
pulse.rules.1: Rest 5 minutes before a resting heart-rate check — avoid talking, caffeine, or recent exercise.
pulse.rules.2: Use light pressure with two fingers. Pressing too hard can change what you feel.
pulse.rules.3: Do not use the thumb to feel the pulse — it has its own pulse and can confuse the count.
pulse.rules.4: After exercise, wait a moment so the first reading is not just movement noise — then tap steadily.
pulse.rules.5: If beats feel irregular, very fast, very slow, or you feel unwell — stop and seek medical advice. This tool is not a diagnosis.
pulse.zones.title: What BPM roughly means
pulse.zones.lead: These are everyday reference bands, not medical targets. Fitness, age, and medication change what’s typical for you.
pulse.zones.light: Light activity: often higher than resting
pulse.zones.exercise: Exercise: can rise well above 100 BPM depending on intensity
pulse.save.title: Save a reading
pulse.save.empty: Tap a stable BPM, type a name, then Save — e.g. Alex — 72 BPM.
pulse.disclaimer: This is a simple tap counter, not a medical device. It does not diagnose, treat, or monitor health conditions. For concerns about your heart rate, talk to a clinician.
pulse.footer.privacy: Pulse taps stay on your device. No accounts. Not medical advice.
pulse.faq.q1: How do I check heart rate without a watch?
pulse.faq.a1: Feel each heartbeat at the wrist or neck and tap along. The tool averages the gaps between taps into beats per minute — so you never need to watch a second hand for a full minute.
pulse.faq.q2: Is an online pulse counter medically accurate?
pulse.faq.a2: No. Accuracy depends on how evenly you tap. Use it for a rough personal check only — not for medical decisions, diagnosis, or treatment.
pulse.faq.q3: What is a typical resting heart rate?
pulse.faq.a3: Many adults rest roughly in the 60–100 BPM range, but “normal” varies by person, fitness, meds, and context. This page does not give medical advice.
pulse.faq.q4: Where should I feel my pulse?
pulse.faq.a4: Common spots are the wrist (thumb-side tendon) and the side of the neck. Use two fingers and light pressure. Skip the thumb.
pulse.faq.q5: Why not just count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4?
pulse.faq.a5: That works if you watch a clock. Tapping skips the clock: each tap marks a beat, and BPM is calculated from the intervals automatically.
pulse.faq.q6: Can I save readings with a name?
pulse.faq.a6: Yes. Enter a name and press Save to store lines like “Alex — 72 BPM” on this device only. Nothing is uploaded.
